name: Palani Murugan Temple
tradition: Kaumaram, the worship of Murugan within the Shaiva tradition
period: Early medieval; a hill shrine of great antiquity
dynasty: Chera and later Pandya, Chola, Nayak
summary: Set atop the Palani hills, the Dhandayuthapani temple is the third of Murugan’s six abodes and among the most visited shrines in Tamil Nadu, its deity a serene renunciant carved from a legendary amalgam of nine minerals.

sections.history: Palani is sung in the Sangam-era Tirumurugatruppadai and has drawn pilgrims for well over a thousand years. Rising on a hill above the plains of the Kongu country, its shrine was patronised across the Chera, Pandya, Chola, and Nayak periods, each leaving its mark on the ascent and the halls below. The temple has long been administered as one of the great pilgrimage centres of the Tamil land, and its hill remains crowned by the abode of the boy-god as an ascetic.
sections.architecture: The temple crowns a hill reached by a long flight of steps, by a winding road, and today by winch-cars and a rope-way. The compact hilltop sanctum enshrines Dhandayuthapani, Murugan as a shaven-headed mendicant holding a staff, said to have been fashioned by the siddha Bogar from an amalgam of nine minerals, the navapashanam. Pillared halls, a golden car, and shrines to the god’s consorts and to Bogar cluster within the walls, while the plains and the town spread out far below the summit.
sections.legends: The temple’s name is bound to the legend of the fruit of wisdom. When the sage Narada offered a single mango, the fruit of knowledge, Shiva set it as a prize for whichever son first circled the world. Murugan mounted his peacock; Ganesha simply walked around his parents, declaring them his world, and won. Slighted, Murugan withdrew to this hill, and Shiva came to console him with the words “pazham nee” — “you yourself are the fruit” — from which Palani takes its name. Here the ardent boy-god stands stripped of ornament, the very image of renunciation.
sections.festivals: Thai Poosam, in the Tamil month of Thai, is Palani’s greatest festival, when vast crowds climb the hill and countless devotees carry the kavadi in fulfilment of vows. Panguni Uthiram, Vaikasi Visakam — the god’s birth star — and Skanda Sashti are all kept with processions and abhishekam. Devotees anoint the mineral image with sandal paste and pancha-amirtham, and the sacred sandal and jaggery prasadam of Palani are carried home across the region as tokens of the pilgrimage.
sections.experience: The climb to Palani is itself an act of devotion, whether by the hundreds of steps, on foot with a kavadi, or by the winch-car that lifts pilgrims to the summit. At the top the air is cooler, the plains stretch to the horizon, and the queue moves toward the small dim sanctum where the mineral image gleams under lamps and fresh sandal. Many shave their heads in vow-fulfilment, and the smell of sandal, camphor, and jasmine hangs over the hilltop as families rest along the parapets after the ascent.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 5:30 am to 9:00 pm daily, with abhishekams through the day; hours extend greatly during Thai Poosam and other festivals.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — dhotis or trousers for men, sarees or salwar kameez for women, shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the foot of the hill or the designated stands.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted around the hilltop sanctum; follow the posted rules and temple staff, especially during festivals and abhishekam.
visit.gettingThere: Palani is in Dindigul district, about 100 km from Madurai and 120 km from Coimbatore, both with airports; the town has its own railway station, and steps, a road, winch-cars, and a rope-way all reach the summit.
